content: A caregiver and child who are willing to participate in a demonstration of a counseling session should be identified. The clinical instructor must also prepare facilitators for their roles during the outpatient session. Facilitators are responsible for pairing participants to work together, arranging the space and furniture for the sessions, and selecting appropriate caregivers and children for the participants to observe and counsel. The selected children should not be severely ill or require hospital referral. A variety of children of different ages and caregiver-child interactions should be included to allow participants to practice diverse skills and activities. Toys should be displayed, cleaned, and returned between sessions. Facilitators should observe participants, provide coaching during initial sessions, and remind them to focus on assisting caregivers rather than directly interacting with the children. Feedback should be given to participants at the end of their sessions, and children should receive any necessary treatments or services promptly after the counseling session. At the beginning of the outpatient session, the purpose and activities should be introduced. Participants will work in pairs, with one counseling the caregiver and the other observing. Both participants should complete a checklist for the child. A facilitator will observe and provide feedback to help participants improve their counseling skills. On the first outpatient session (Day 2), participants will practice greeting caregivers and children, asking questions, observing caregiver-child interactions, praising caregivers, and advising them. They will use a checklist to guide the counseling process and counseling cards to identify suitable play and communication activities. On Day 3, participants will also assist caregivers in solving problems related to providing care at home. A demonstration of a counseling session with a caregiver and child should be conducted. During the demonstration, participants should record information on the checklist. The demonstration should include the following steps: warmly greet the caregiver, interview the caregiver to complete the checklist, observe the caregiver-child interaction, and note observations without commenting until after the session. Participants should complete the checklist, noting how the caregiver responds to the child’s movements, comforts the child, shows love, and corrects the child. Questions should be asked to understand how the caregiver plays and communicates with the child and their perception of the child’s development. Specific questions include: “How do you play with your child?”, “How do you talk with your child?”, “How do you get your child to smile?”, and “How do you think your child is learning?” The caregiver should be praised for specific positive actions and advised on play and communication activities to do at home. The caregiver should be coached on how to get the child’s attention, identify and respond to the child’s cues, and engage in age-appropriate activities. Recommendations for play and communication should be explained in terms of how they will help the child grow and learn. The caregiver’s understanding should be checked by observing them try the activity and helping them apply it to home activities. On Day 3, participants should ask about any challenges the caregiver faced in playing and communicating with the child at home and help them solve these problems. At the end of the demonstration, after the caregiver and child leave, the counseling session should be discussed. Questions to discuss include: which activities were selected and why, how the caregiver and child responded, and how the session could be improved. On Day 3, additional questions should help participants observe caregiver-child interactions, such as whether the caregiver was sensitive to the child’s cues, how appropriate their responses were, and whether there was a connection between the caregiver and child. Participants should also reflect on how the counselor strengthened caregiver-child interactions and how these interactions might affect the child’s survival and learning. Facilitators should add their observations if necessary. Participants should then practice counseling caregivers. Facilitators should bring a caregiver and child to each pair of participants. The counseling sessions should be observed, and feedback provided to participants to improve their skills. Notes should be taken on the sessions to debrief participants on their experiences with caregivers and children. At the end of the counseling session, participants should return to the classroom for debriefing. After a break, four or five examples of caregiver-child interactions observed during the session should be discussed, including good interactions (e.g., caregiver awareness of the child and sensitivity to cues, child looking at the caregiver) and poor interactions (e.g., little connection between caregiver and child). Other characteristics, such as the child’s level of activity, happiness, and responsiveness, should also be discussed. Changes in caregiver-child interactions during the activities should be noted. On Day 3, problems caregivers identified in doing activities at home and how participants helped solve them should be discussed. Participants should also reflect on what was easy or difficult for them to do. If available, photos or videos from the session can be used to illustrate discussion points. Facilitators should meet at the end of each day to discuss the day’s progress and prepare for the next day. The clinical instructor should summarize each participant’s progress. Facilitators should discuss how well participants are performing in the classroom and clinical practice, any difficulties they are experiencing, and potential solutions. Solutions may include assigning a facilitator to work closely with participants who are struggling, pairing stronger participants with weaker ones, reviewing skills in the classroom before the next clinical session, or improving the preparation and organization of clinical sessions to allow for more supervised practice. During inpatient sessions, demonstrations should include approaching a sick child, gaining the child’s attention, following the child’s lead, playing and communicating with the child using age-appropriate activities and toys, increasing the child’s activity level and use of new skills, and praising the child for their efforts. Grand rounds should involve presenting two or three sample children and discussing what happened during the interaction, how the child’s attention was gained, how the child’s lead was followed, the chosen play or communication activity and its rationale, the child’s response, and any changes in the child’s activity level or learning. Counselors should demonstrate one activity. Debriefing should summarize skills such as approaching the child, gaining their attention, following their lead, playing and communicating, increasing activity levels, and praising the child. Activities appropriate for sick children and their rationale should also be discussed.
